name: Beth Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, have a master’s degree and lead dialysis-scheduling software at a small tech company. I am among the strongest developers here and use AI occasionally to understand older code, but I check treatment slots with the clinic roster. Amal works bakery shifts, our children are grown, and below-market lead pay, rent and my mother’s care leave us about three weeks saved with few similar local jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the dialysis-scheduling team that a little AI can sort a repeated request, but a patient still needs the correct treatment slot. I use AI occasionally to explain an old function and then check the clinic calendar myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58, have a master’s degree and lead the software team at a small tech company. I am good at tracing missed appointments, but the firm pays below the usual lead rate; Amal works part-time in a bakery, our children are grown, and rent plus my mother’s care costs leave us about three weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing the treatment-slot code and compare one clinic exception report each Friday. We would stop ordering weekend meals and save 35 monthly only when both wages and my mother’s care costs allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious even if AI makes only small changes. A delayed pay cheque or extra care bill could consume our whole reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a missed slot cause?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A patient was offered a chair after the clinic had closed its late shift. I compared the booking record with the nurse’s roster before anyone travelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why stay at lower pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother’s care is nearby, and there are few other software firms in reach. I have asked for a raise, but I cannot put one in next month’s budget.

I want **clinic exceptions** reviewed by our team before a schedule is released.
think: I have **three weeks saved** despite senior skill.
I worry about **care costs and rent** on lower lead pay.

**Stop weekend meal orders**; save 35 only when wages and care costs allow.
feel: **Anxious** about current care bills and rent.

The **care-cost pressure** keeps the plateau anxious even with stable software demand and a highly skilled lead role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking booking, checking, coding and patient replies could thin the scheduling team. The clinic should still know which person owns a missed treatment slot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead role could shrink if one person oversees several automated clinics. With three weeks saved and care costs that cannot wait, I would feel any cut in pay quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the manager this month for a written staffing plan and approved paid time to learn the new AI scheduling test on invented patient accounts. If approved, I’d check one false double booking weekly with a nurse; if lead hours are cut, I’d search paid local clinical-software vacancies only if wages cover rent and care bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own wage, though testing a new tool is sensible. A fast calendar can still send a sick person to a closed door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the nurse check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The nurse would compare the fake booking with the actual treatment roster rules. No real patient name would enter the training file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if paid time is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep reviewing current code and ask for written notice of hours changes. I would not call watching an unapproved demo new training.

I want **written staffing numbers** for our lead team.
think: I could lose **paid lead hours** if one developer oversees several automated clinics.
I cannot bridge **care bills** and rent with only three weeks saved.
do: **Request staffing plan**; learn AI test weekly only with approved paid time, fake accounts and nurse review.
**Search paid clinical software** if lead hours fall and local vacancies cover rent and care bills.
feel: **Anxious** about own wage and patient harm.
S1.quote: A fast calendar can still send a sick person to a closed door.
fieldNote: She learns **a new AI test** beyond occasional code explanations, on paid synthetic records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write scheduling code and answer clinic calls more cheaply than our team. Robots moving patients and working in bakeries may follow around 2031, after our screen work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead developer job could end despite my experience. Three weeks saved would not pay rent and my mother’s care for long, and Amal’s bakery shifts alone would not cover both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d stop ordering weekend meals and ask for written notice of any lead cuts now. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local clinic-record quality openings only if they exist, I meet the requirements and wages cover rent and care bills; I would ask the public employment office what help our household actually qualifies for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about losing the wage that covers care. A clean clinic record does not pay the nurse who comes to my mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children pay for care?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not budget for that. They visit their grandmother, but they have their own rent and jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would record work survive AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know. I would take only a real paid opening and keep searching if the work shrank.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach scheduling code first.
I expect **care robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **lead developer wage** could end.
I cannot cover **rent and care** from three weeks saved.
do: **Stop weekend meals** and request written cut notice now.
**Apply for clinic-quality openings** after 2028 loss only if qualified paid local vacancies cover rent and care.
**Ask public employment office** about actual household eligibility if displaced.
S2.quote: A clean clinic record does not pay the nurse who comes to my mother.
fieldNote: Her **care costs** are an existing household obligation, not a hypothetical future expense.
The **quality-role fallback** requires qualification and an actual paid opening covering rent and care.

steps.text: Stop ordering weekend meals when lead developer cuts threaten
Apply for qualified paid local clinic-quality vacancies after 2028 job loss if wages cover rent, care

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives us time to check how a missed treatment slot is investigated before code changes. Robots helping patients move may follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn the clinic’s incident-review process while keeping my developer wage, though AGI may do much of the paperwork. I cannot pay for an outside course while our care reserve is three weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my employer and the clinic manager for a paid monthly review of one anonymized missed-slot incident with a nurse supervisor. If both approve paid time, I’d practise tracing the booking and roster; we would save 40 monthly only while both wages and care costs allow, and after 2031 job loss I’d apply for paid local clinic-quality vacancies only if qualified and wages cover rent and care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about the lead job but able to test a real care process. A missed chair is a person’s treatment day, not a row in my table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you trace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the patient-free booking record, the staffing roster and the message sent to the clinic. The nurse supervisor would tell me which safety step I missed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the clinic refuses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the software role and read public clinical guidance. I would not call an unapproved meeting supervised training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 gives clinics time to keep clear treatment records and families time to calculate costs. Robots moving patients may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may still need paid work at 68, and I have not verified a retirement amount. The care bill and three-week reserve make me anxious now even if a decade gives me time to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing treatment schedules and ask for a written retirement-income estimate this year. We would save 45 monthly only while both wages and my mother’s care costs allow; if my developer job ends after 2036, I’d seek paid local clinic-quality vacancies only if qualified and wages cover rent and care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d remain anxious about current money, not only the distant job. A ten-year forecast cannot pay next month’s care bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for clinic work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would search local clinics and software firms first. My mother’s care and Amal’s bakery shifts are here, so I am not planning a move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the estimate change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare it with rent and care before setting a date to stop work. I would not count an unverified benefit as income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my lead wage could end while rent and my mother’s care continue. Written notice, a qualified local paid clinic opening and verified public help would give us a route through it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether my children would pay their grandmother’s care bill. I will not build our rent plan on my children’s wages or a benefit no office has confirmed.

headlineQuote: I will not build our rent plan on my children’s wages or a benefit no office has confirmed.
portrait: Beth is a **58-year-old software lead** with a master’s degree, lower pay and three weeks saved.
She and Amal **rent** while paying for her mother’s care; their grown children have separate households.
She **uses AI occasionally** but checks treatment slots against nurse rosters.
She seeks **paid clinical incident learning** only with both employers’ approval and nurse supervision.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her care-paying lead wage before another paid opening appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a qualified local vacancy and verified public support would help.
